title: Working Papers
text:
Working Papers

A Strategic Environment:  
Community Conservation, Site Selection, and Spillovers in Eastern Zambia  Revise and Resubmit, Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists (JAERE)







Draft







Abstract






I study how strategic site selection and spatial spillovers shape the effectiveness of a USAID-funded conservation project in Eastern Zambia. Using satellite and administrative data at the 1 km × 1 km grid level from 2001 to 2023, I employ a Difference-in-Differences design with propensity-score-matched controls. For Participating Chiefdoms, tree cover loss fell by 0.14–0.15 percentage points within Conservation Areas, with no leakage into adjacent Communal Lands. For Non-Participating Chiefdoms, areas close to conservation boundaries exhibit spillover reductions of 0.17–0.19 percentage points, with no effects in far areas. In hectares, these effects correspond to yearly avoided deforestation of 753–866 ha and 6,777–7,794 ha. Conservation effects were strongest near roads and human settlements. I also document selection bias by showing that Conservation Areas were disproportionately placed in remote, low-deforestation locations, limiting aggregate impact. These findings highlight the importance of spatial targeting and incentive diffusion beyond formal boundaries.





Air Pollution Burden Around the World:  Distributions, Inequalities, and the Economic Benefits of Clean Air  with Jere Behrman, Emily Hannum, Oscar Morales, and Fan Wang


 
Draft   Poster







Abstract






We construct a globally harmonized, high-resolution dataset combining satellite-based aerosol optical depth (AOD) and population data to document global inequalities in air pollution exposure. By weighting pollution by population shares, we provide one of the first comprehensive assessments of how exposure to air pollution by aerosols varies across and within countries and regions. We find large disparities: populations in Asia face average exposure levels more than three times higher than those in Oceania, and within-country inequalities reach up to 359%. Our analysis reveals compounding inequalities—regions with higher pollution also tend to be poorer, with double-ratio metrics indicating that environmental disadvantage amplifies economic inequality. Finally, we provide the first Global Compensating Equivalent Variation (CEV) estimate for clean air, finding that welfare gains from cleaner air exceed 10% of GDP in many highly polluted areas, underscoring the significant economic and social returns from targeted pollution abatement policies.





Increasing Pollution, Increasing Heat, and Rapid Rise of Compound Environmental Risks for Latin American and Caribbean Children  with Jere R. Behrman, Emily Hannum, Oscar Morales, and Fan Wang


 
Draft   Poster







Abstract






Globally, air pollution and extreme heat pose important risks to human health and wellbeing, and children are particularly vulnerable to these hazards. We analyze how ambient exposures to these hazards are distributed across, and overlap with, the young child population of Latin America and the Caribbean. We then compare ambient exposure across income, human development, remoteness, urbanicity, and Indigenous land, and track how it changed between 2000 and 2020. Our findings highlight substantial increases in the mean and in the dispersion of ambient exposures from 2000 to 2020. Compared with 2000, in 2020 an additional 7.9 million children were exposed to air pollution above \(10 \mu g/m^{3}\), the World Health Organization limit for safe exposure until 2021. For heat stress, 3.5 million additional children were exposed to a Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI) above 32°C for at least 3 months of the year. Beyond increases in single-hazard ambient exposures, we find growing compound exposures. In 2020, 4.3 million children (9.2% of the child population) were exposed to both \(PM_{2.5}\) above \(15 \mu g/m^{3}\) and at least 3 months of extreme heat, 3.2 million more than in 2000. Moreover, poorer, less developed, more remote, and more rural areas face both the highest compound exposure and the largest increases since 2000. These findings show that ambient exposure compounds socioeconomic and geographic disadvantages and threatens young children’s health and wellbeing.






Unfolding the Greener Path: A Global Subnational Analysis of the Environmental Kuznets Curve  with Oscar Morales, Jere R. Behrman, Emily Hannum, and Fan Wang







Draft






Abstract






This paper provides the first global subnational analysis of the Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC), relating GDP per capita and air pollution by aerosol. We use satellite data for Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD), a proxy for air pollution, and merge it with subnational GDP per capita for 2010 and population estimates. Our polynomial and quantile regressions confirm a robust inverted U-shaped relationship between income and pollution globally. However, we find significant heterogeneity across the air pollution distribution, with lower pollution quantiles exhibiting a flatter curve than higher pollution ones. Estimated Pollution-GDP elasticities confirm the overall EKC trend globally, with poorer regions exhibiting positive elasticities, while richer regions show negative magnitudes. However, considerable variation exists within regions, emphasizing that the development-pollution trajectory is not uniform.





Dynamic Fertility Intentions in the Aftermath of a Flood  with Leticia J. Marteleto, Alexandre Gori Maia







Draft coming soon…






Abstract






In this paper, we examine how fertility intentions evolved in response to a weather shock. We leverage spatiotemporal variation in exposure to and impact of a massive flash flood that occurred during panel surveys in 2020 and 2021, using a population-based sample of 2,520 women aged 18–34 across 94 municipalities in Pernambuco, Brazil. We use individual fixed-effects regressions to examine whether exposure to and impact of the 2022 flood are associated with changes in women’s fertility intentions, net of time-varying sociodemographic factors. We find important differences between exposure and impact. Findings show that traditional contextual measures of exposure to flood do not change fertility intentions, but a more nuanced measure that captures flood impact and resilience at the individual level suggests that women move towards postponing and foregoing. These innovative findings suggest that women affected by the 2022 flood loss within their communities intend to to build and consolidate their families. We advance knowledge about varying contextual influences on fertility preferences in the aftermath of weather shocks in a middle-income country with relatively young and below-replacement fertility.

title: Strategic Environment: Conservation Policies Effectiveness and Strategic Behavior
text:
Draft










Conservation area policies are crucial for preserving natural resources. Using a REDD+ project funded by USAID in Eastern Zambia, I investigate the impact of community compensation on environmental outcomes. By analyzing Chiefdom and household data, I explore how forest dependence and social norms influence conservation performance. The protected area boundaries were established with local authorities, potentially leading to strategic site selection. Leveraging geospatial and household data, I assess whether communities strategically selected low-pressure areas for protection. My findings show no reduction in deforestation within protected areas but suggest negative spillover effects in non-protected areas. Non-protected areas increase tree cover loss after the policy, which lead to overall deforestation rates increased in treated chiefdoms post-policy. This research highlights the need to account for incentives and strategic behavior when designing effective conservation policies.

title: Angelo dos Santos
text:
Welcome!

I am a Postdoctoral Fellow and Penn Climate Scholars Fellow at the University of Pennsylvania. I am also the Scientific Production Coordinator for the DZC project.
I am an applied microeconomist working on development and environmental economics.
My research spans two broad areas: the drivers and governance of deforestation; and the effects of environmental exposures on human development, including the role of climate adaptation in mitigating them.
Outside of research, I love spending time in nature and playing football.
